Part 1c: from a point to a distribution

Machine learning and inversion for seismologists

Physics from Parts 1a and 1b, unchanged:
def travel_times(m_x, m_y, xi_x, xi_y, v_ref):
    """Forward operator F(m; xi): straight rays at constant P speed.

    m_x, m_y: source coordinates (km), tensors of shape (...)
    xi_x, xi_y: station coordinates (km), shape (N,)
    v_ref: P speed (km/s)
    returns: travel time (s) from every source to every station, shape (..., N)
    """
    delta_x = m_x[..., None] - xi_x
    delta_y = m_y[..., None] - xi_y
    Delta = torch.sqrt(delta_x**2 + delta_y**2)
    return Delta / v_ref


def center(d):
    """Station-mean projection C d = d - <d>: removes the origin time t0.

    d: (..., N) times (s), either picks or travel times
    returns: centred times, shape (..., N), with zero mean over the stations
    """
    return d - d.mean(-1, keepdim=True)


def observe(F, m, sigma, live):
    """Centred noisy picks d~ = C (F(m) + eps): what the locator network sees.

    F: forward operator, F(m_x, m_y) -> travel times (s), shape (n, N)
    m: sources (km), shape (n, 2)
    sigma: standard deviation of a pick (s)
    live: which stations work, bool, shape (N,); a muted station is left out of the
        mean and reads 0
    returns: centred picks (s), shape (n, N)
    """
    F_m = F(m[:, 0], m[:, 1])
    d = F_m + sigma * torch.randn(F_m.shape, dtype=F_m.dtype)
    d_c = d - d[:, live].mean(-1, keepdim=True)
    return d_c * live

data.text/markdown:
The loss picks the summary

The posterior ||(p(\mathbf{m} \mid \tilde{\mathbf{d}})||) describes how likely it is for the source to be at ||(\mathbf{m}||) given our prior knowledge and what we measured. A network outputs one point ||(\hat{\mathbf{m}}||), so the loss decides which point: training minimises the expected loss ||(S(\hat{\mathbf{m}})||), with ||(\mathbb{E}||) the average over sources ||(\mathbf{m}||) drawn from the posterior. MSE (mean squared error): big misses cost far more than small ones ||[ S(\hat{\mathbf{m}}) = \mathbb{E}\left[\lVert \mathbf{m} - \hat{\mathbf{m}} \rVert^2_2 \right] \quad\Rightarrow\quad \hat{\mathbf{m}} = \mathbb{E}[\mathbf{m}] ||]The mean. With two lobes it lands between them, where the source is not. MAE (mean absolute error): a miss costs in proportion to its size ||[ S(\hat{\mathbf{m}}) = \mathbb{E}\left[\lVert \mathbf{m} - \hat{\mathbf{m}} \rVert_1\right] \quad\Rightarrow\quad \hat{\mathbf{m}} = \operatorname{median}[\mathbf{m}] ||]The median, of ||(m_x||) and ||(m_y||) separately: half of the posterior lies on either side. With two lobes it sits inside one. MAP (maximum a posteriori): no averaging. With prior density ||(\rho_M||) from before ||[ \hat{\mathbf{m}} = \arg\min_{\mathbf{m}} \left[\frac{S(\mathbf{m})}{\sigma^2} - \log \rho_M(\mathbf{m})\right] \quad\Rightarrow\quad \hat{\mathbf{m}} = \arg\max_{\mathbf{m}}\, p(\mathbf{m} \mid \tilde{\mathbf{d}}) ||]The highest peak of the posterior. If the posterior is one symmetric peak, all three agree. For multimodal distributions they do not, and none of them is wrong, they answer different questions. No single point can say "it is either here or there": that needs the whole density, which is what we learn next.

A Gaussian mixture

Describe the answer as a density: ||(K||) Gaussian bumps, ||[ q(\mathbf{m}) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} w_k\, \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{m};\, \boldsymbol{\mu}_k, \mathbf{L}_k \mathbf{L}_k^\top), \qquad \mathbf{w} = \operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf{a}) ||]Per component: one logit ||(a_k||), two numbers for the mean, three for the lower-triangular ||(\mathbf{L}_k||). 6 x K numbers in total. The loss is the negative log-likelihood of the truth, ||[ S = -\frac{1}{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} \log q(\mathbf{m}_j) ||]which is small only when ||(q||) puts its mass on the true locations.

(() => {
  const it = c => {
    const k = c.codePointAt(0);
    if (k >= 65 && k <= 90) return String.fromCodePoint(0x1D434 + k - 65);
    if (k >= 97 && k <= 122)
      return k === 104 ? "\u210E" : String.fromCodePoint(0x1D44E + k - 97);
    if (k >= 0x391 && k <= 0x3A9) return String.fromCodePoint(0x1D6E2 + k - 0x391);
    if (k >= 0x3B1 && k <= 0x3C9) return String.fromCodePoint(0x1D6FC + k - 0x3B1);
    return c;
  };
  const fix = n => {
    const p = n.parentElement;
    if (!p || !p.closest(".m, .sym")) return;
    const u = Array.from(n.nodeValue, it).join("");
    if (u !== n.nodeValue) n.nodeValue = u;
  };
  const walk = root => {
    if (root.nodeType === 3) return fix(root);
    const w = document.createTreeWalker(root, NodeFilter.SHOW_TEXT);
    for (let n = w.nextNode(); n; n = w.nextNode()) fix(n);
  };
  new MutationObserver(ms => ms.forEach(m => {
    if (m.type === "characterData") fix(m.target); else m.addedNodes.forEach(walk);
  })).observe(document, { childList: true, subtree: true, characterData: true });
  document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", () => walk(document.body));
})();

<script>
const BOX = 100, SIDE = 424, PAD = { l: 44, t: 8, b: 34 };
const css = (v) => getComputedStyle(document.documentElement).getPropertyValue(v).trim();
const COLS = ["--c1", "--c3", "--c5", "--c4"];  // one hue per component; vermillion is the event
const START = [
  { a: 0.3, mu: [72, 66], L: [6, 6, 5] },
  { a: 0.0, mu: [74, 34], L: [5, -6, 6] },
  { a: -1.0, mu: [35, 70], L: [9, 0, 4] },
  { a: -1.5, mu: [30, 25], L: [4, 2, 9] },
];
let comps = START.slice(0, 2).map((c) => structuredClone(c));
let star = [76, 62], drag = null;

const cv = document.getElementById("map"), ctx = cv.getContext("2d");
const W = PAD.l + SIDE + 10, H = PAD.t + SIDE + PAD.b;
function sizeCanvas() {  // sharp at any stage scale (set by the host, see ml_seis.slides)
  const res = (window.devicePixelRatio || 1) * (window.STAGE_SCALE || 1);
  cv.width = Math.round(W * res); cv.height = Math.round(H * res);
  cv.style.width = W + "px"; cv.style.height = H + "px";
  ctx.setTransform(res, 0, 0, res, 0, 0);
}
sizeCanvas();
const X = (x) => PAD.l + x / BOX * SIDE, Y = (y) => PAD.t + SIDE - y / BOX * SIDE;
const kmX = (px) => (px - PAD.l) / SIDE * BOX, kmY = (py) => (PAD.t + SIDE - py) / SIDE * BOX;

function weights() {
  const m = Math.max(...comps.map((c) => c.a)), e = comps.map((c) => Math.exp(c.a - m));
  const s = e.reduce((p, q) => p + q, 0);
  return e.map((v) => v / s);
}
function parts_at(x, y) {  // w_k N(m; mu_k, L_k L_k^T) in 1/km², one entry per component
  const w = weights();
  return comps.map((c, k) => {
    const [l11, l21, l22] = c.L;
    const u = (x - c.mu[0]) / l11, v = (y - c.mu[1] - l21 * u) / l22;  // L^-1 (m - mu)
    return w[k] * Math.exp(-0.5 * (u * u + v * v)) / (2 * Math.PI * l11 * l22);
  });
}
const density = (x, y) => parts_at(x, y).reduce((p, q) => p + q, 0);  // q(m) in 1/km²

const N = 110, img = document.createElement("canvas");
img.width = N; img.height = N;
function shade() {
  const g = img.getContext("2d"), im = g.createImageData(N, N), vals = [], resp = [];
  let mx = 1e-12;
  for (let j = 0; j < N; j++) for (let i = 0; i < N; i++) {
    const x = (i + 0.5) / N * BOX, y = (N - j - 0.5) / N * BOX, parts = parts_at(x, y);
    const v = parts.reduce((p, q) => p + q, 0);
    vals.push(v); resp.push(parts.map((q) => q / Math.max(v, 1e-300))); mx = Math.max(mx, v);
  }
  const rgb = (v) => css(v).match(/\w\w/g).map((h) => parseInt(h, 16));
  const bg = rgb("--bg"), cols = comps.map((_, k) => rgb(COLS[k]));
  vals.forEach((v, p) => {  // hue: the component that owns the pixel, strength: q
    const f = Math.pow(v / mx, 0.6), r = resp[p];
    for (let c = 0; c < 3; c++) {
      let h = 0;
      for (let k = 0; k < cols.length; k++) h += r[k] * cols[k][c];
      im.data[4 * p + c] = Math.round(bg[c] + (h - bg[c]) * 0.85 * f);
    }
    im.data[4 * p + 3] = 255;
  });
  g.putImageData(im, 0, 0);
}

function handles(c) {
  const [l11, l21, l22] = c.L;
  return { mu: c.mu, col1: [c.mu[0] + l11, c.mu[1] + l21], col2: [c.mu[0], c.mu[1] + l22] };
}
function draw() {
  shade();
  ctx.clearRect(0, 0, W, H);
  ctx.imageSmoothingEnabled = true;
  ctx.drawImage(img, X(0), Y(BOX), SIDE, SIDE);
  ctx.strokeStyle = css("--ink2"); ctx.lineWidth = 1; ctx.strokeRect(X(0), Y(BOX), SIDE, SIDE);
  ctx.fillStyle = css("--ink"); ctx.font = "12px DejaVu Sans, sans-serif";
  for (let v = 0; v <= BOX; v += 10) {  // inward ticks on all four sides, labels every 20 km
    const major = v % 20 === 0, t = major ? 6 : 3;
    ctx.beginPath();
    ctx.moveTo(X(v), Y(0)); ctx.lineTo(X(v), Y(0) - t);
    ctx.moveTo(X(v), Y(BOX)); ctx.lineTo(X(v), Y(BOX) + t);
    ctx.moveTo(X(0), Y(v)); ctx.lineTo(X(0) + t, Y(v));
    ctx.moveTo(X(BOX), Y(v)); ctx.lineTo(X(BOX) - t, Y(v));
    ctx.stroke();
    if (!major) continue;
    ctx.textAlign = "center"; ctx.fillText(v, X(v), Y(0) + 16);
    ctx.textAlign = "right"; ctx.fillText(v, X(0) - 6, Y(v) + 4);
  }
  const axisLabel = (x, y, sub) => {  // m_x (km), m_y (km): math italic, unit upright
    ctx.textAlign = "left"; ctx.font = '16px "Latin Modern Math", serif';
    const w1 = ctx.measureText("\u{1D45A}").width, w2 = ctx.measureText(" (km)").width;
    ctx.font = '11px "Latin Modern Math", serif';
    const ws = ctx.measureText(sub).width, x0 = x - (w1 + ws + w2 + 4) / 2;
    ctx.font = '16px "Latin Modern Math", serif'; ctx.fillText("\u{1D45A}", x0, y);
    ctx.font = '11px "Latin Modern Math", serif'; ctx.fillText(sub, x0 + w1, y + 4);
    ctx.font = "12px DejaVu Sans, sans-serif"; ctx.fillText(" (km)", x0 + w1 + ws + 2, y);
  };
  axisLabel(X(BOX / 2), Y(0) + 31, "\u{1D465}");
  ctx.save(); ctx.translate(12, Y(BOX / 2)); ctx.rotate(-Math.PI / 2);
  axisLabel(0, 0, "\u{1D466}"); ctx.restore();
  ctx.save(); ctx.beginPath(); ctx.rect(X(0), Y(BOX), SIDE, SIDE); ctx.clip();
  comps.forEach((c, k) => {
    const col = css(COLS[k]), h = handles(c), [l11, l21, l22] = c.L;
    ctx.strokeStyle = col;
    for (const [n, dash, lw] of [[2, [4, 3], 1], [1, [], 1.8]]) {  // n-sigma ellipses: mu + n L (cos, sin)
      ctx.lineWidth = lw; ctx.setLineDash(dash); ctx.beginPath();
      for (let t = 0; t <= 64; t++) {
        const u = n * Math.cos(t / 64 * 2 * Math.PI), v = n * Math.sin(t / 64 * 2 * Math.PI);
        const p = [X(c.mu[0] + l11 * u), Y(c.mu[1] + l21 * u + l22 * v)];
        t ? ctx.lineTo(...p) : ctx.moveTo(...p);
      }
      ctx.stroke();
    }
    ctx.setLineDash([]); ctx.lineWidth = 1.2;
    for (const end of [h.col1, h.col2]) {
      ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(X(c.mu[0]), Y(c.mu[1])); ctx.lineTo(X(end[0]), Y(end[1])); ctx.stroke();
    }
    ctx.fillStyle = col;
    ctx.fillRect(X(h.col1[0]) - 5, Y(h.col1[1]) - 5, 10, 10);
    ctx.beginPath(); ctx.moveTo(X(h.col2[0]), Y(h.col2[1]) - 7);
    ctx.lineTo(X(h.col2[0]) + 6, Y(h.col2[1]) + 4); ctx.lineTo(X(h.col2[0]) - 6, Y(h.col2[1]) + 4);
    ctx.fill();
    ctx.beginPath(); ctx.arc(X(c.mu[0]), Y(c.mu[1]), 8, 0, 7); ctx.fill();
    ctx.strokeStyle = css("--bg"); ctx.lineWidth = 1.5; ctx.stroke();
    ctx.fillStyle = css("--bg"); ctx.font = "11px DejaVu Sans, sans-serif"; ctx.textAlign = "center";
    ctx.fillText(k + 1, X(c.mu[0]), Y(c.mu[1]) + 4);
  });
  starMark(X(star[0]), Y(star[1]));
  ctx.restore();
  ctx.font = "11px DejaVu Sans, sans-serif"; ctx.textAlign = "left"; ctx.fillStyle = css("--ink2");
  ctx.fillText("solid 1σ, dashed 2σ", X(0) + 8, Y(BOX) + 16);
  panel();
}
function starMark(x, y) {
  ctx.beginPath();
  for (let i = 0; i < 10; i++) {
    const a = -Math.PI / 2 + i * Math.PI / 5, r = i % 2 ? 4.6 : 11;
    ctx[i ? "lineTo" : "moveTo"](x + r * Math.cos(a), y + r * Math.sin(a));
  }
  ctx.closePath(); ctx.fillStyle = css("--c2"); ctx.fill();
  ctx.strokeStyle = css("--bg"); ctx.lineWidth = 1.2; ctx.stroke();
}

const fmt = (v) => (Math.abs(v) >= 10 ? v.toFixed(0) : v.toFixed(1));
function panel() {
  const K = comps.length, w = weights();
  document.getElementById("stripHead").textContent = `the network's output: 6K = ${6 * K} numbers`;
  const groups = [
    ["logits a", comps.map((c, k) => [[c.a, k]])],
    ["means μ (km)", comps.map((c, k) => [[c.mu[0], k], [c.mu[1], k]])],
    ["L₁₁, L₂₁, L₂₂ (km)", comps.map((c, k) => c.L.map((v) => [v, k]))],
  ];
  const strip = document.getElementById("strip");
  strip.replaceChildren();
  for (const [label, parts] of groups) {
    const g = document.createElement("div"); g.className = "grp";
    g.innerHTML = `<div class="lab">${label}</div>`;
    const cells = document.createElement("div"); cells.className = "cells";
    for (const [v, k] of parts.flat()) {
      const c = document.createElement("div"); c.className = "cell";
      c.style.borderColor = css(COLS[k]); c.textContent = fmt(v); cells.append(c);
    }
    g.append(cells); strip.append(g);
  }
  const table = document.getElementById("weights");
  if (table.rows.length !== K) {
    table.replaceChildren();
    comps.forEach((c, k) => {
      const r = table.insertRow();
      r.innerHTML = `<td><span class="dot" style="background:${css(COLS[k])}"></span></td>
        <td class="sym">a<sub>${k + 1}</sub></td><td><input type="range" min="-3" max="3" step="0.05"></td>
        <td class="sym">w<sub>${k + 1}</sub></td><td class="wv mono"></td>
        <td><span class="wbar" style="background:${css(COLS[k])}"></span></td>`;
      const s = r.querySelector("input"); s.style.setProperty("--col", css(COLS[k]));
      s.value = c.a;
      s.oninput = () => { c.a = +s.value; draw(); };
    });
  }
  [...table.rows].forEach((r, k) => {
    r.querySelector(".wv").textContent = "= " + w[k].toFixed(2);
    r.querySelector(".wbar").style.width = Math.round(120 * w[k]) + "px";
  });
  document.getElementById("kval").textContent = K;
  document.getElementById("minus").disabled = K <= 1;
  document.getElementById("plus").disabled = K >= START.length;
  const nll = -Math.log(Math.max(density(...star), 1e-300));
  document.getElementById("nll").innerHTML =
    `<span style="color:${css("--c2")}">★</span> loss −log <span class="sym">q</span> = <span class="mono" style="color:${css("--c2")}">${nll.toFixed(2)}</span>`;
}

function hit(px, py) {
  const d = (p) => Math.hypot(X(p[0]) - px, Y(p[1]) - py);
  if (d(star) < 13) return { kind: "star" };
  for (let k = comps.length - 1; k >= 0; k--) {
    const h = handles(comps[k]);
    for (const part of ["col1", "col2", "mu"]) if (d(h[part]) < 11) return { kind: part, k };
  }
  return null;
}
function xy(e) {
  const r = cv.getBoundingClientRect(), s = r.width / W;
  return [(e.clientX - r.left) / s, (e.clientY - r.top) / s];
}
const clamp = (v, lo, hi) => Math.min(hi, Math.max(lo, v));
cv.addEventListener("pointerdown", (e) => {
  drag = hit(...xy(e));
  if (drag) cv.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId);
});
cv.addEventListener("pointermove", (e) => {
  const [px, py] = xy(e);
  if (!drag) { cv.style.cursor = hit(px, py) ? "grab" : "default"; return; }
  const x = clamp(kmX(px), 0, BOX), y = clamp(kmY(py), 0, BOX);
  if (drag.kind === "star") star = [x, y];
  else {
    const c = comps[drag.k];
    if (drag.kind === "mu") c.mu = [x, y];
    if (drag.kind === "col1") { c.L[0] = Math.max(1, x - c.mu[0]); c.L[1] = y - c.mu[1]; }
    if (drag.kind === "col2") c.L[2] = Math.max(1, y - c.mu[1]);
  }
  draw();
});
const release = () => { drag = null; };
cv.addEventListener("pointerup", release);
cv.addEventListener("pointercancel", release);
document.getElementById("plus").onclick = () => {
  if (comps.length < START.length) { comps.push(structuredClone(START[comps.length])); draw(); }
};
document.getElementById("minus").onclick = () => {
  if (comps.length > 1) { comps.pop(); draw(); }
};
window.addEventListener("stagefit", () => { sizeCanvas(); draw(); });

draw();
</script>
</body>
</html>

data.text/markdown:
Fit a mixture to one posterior

No network yet. The target is a multimodal posterior: the same five stations, but a heterogeneous velocity model, so the data constrain the source along a curved band with several clusters rather than two clean lobes (flat prior). Fit ||(q||) to samples of it by gradient descent on the NLL. Keep 2000 more samples apart: they play the role of the validation events, and the NLL on them is how well ||(q||) carries over to samples it was not fitted to.

data.text/html:
Three things to look for

  • One against several. What does a single component do to a curved band with several clusters?
  • Fitted against held out. How do the NLL of the fitted and of the held-out samples change as ||(K||) grows, and where do they part?
  • Few against many. What do few fitted samples do that many do not?

Setup. Slider ||(K||) = 1, then 2, 3, 4. Look for. ||(K||) = 1: one wide ellipse laid over the band, covering much empty ground. Each added component follows the curve better.
Setup. Move ||(K||) from 1 to 12 and read the two NLL curves. Look for. Both curves fall until about ||(K||) = 4. After that the fitted NLL keeps creeping down while the held-out NLL stops improving and rises: the extra components learn the fitted samples, not the density.
Setup. Slider SAMPLES = 25 with ||(K||) = 8, then SAMPLES = 1600. Look for. 25: the fitted NLL falls to 5.2 while the held-out NLL runs away to 29 — the 8 components learn the 25 samples, not the density. 1600: the two curves stay close for every ||(K||).

data.text/markdown:
Let the network output the mixture

The last layer now gives ||(6K||) numbers instead of two, so every set of picks gets its own mixture ||(q(\mathbf{m} \mid \tilde{\mathbf{d}})||): a mixture density network. Two lines of the training loop change, the output size and the loss, ||[ S = -\frac{1}{n} \sum_{j=1}^{n} \log q(\mathbf{m}_j \mid \tilde{\mathbf{d}}_j) ||]which is smallest when ||(q||) is the posterior.

data.text/html:
Four things to look for

Change one thing at a time and watch the maps, the curves and the errors.
  • Output. What does the network return when the data allow two answers?
  • Components. How many bumps does the answer need?
  • Ambiguity. What happens to the answer as the event moves towards the line of stations, and away from it?
  • Shift. Does the spread of the mixture tell you when the network is out of its depth?

data.text/markdown:
How the playground works

The playground of 1b again, on the line of stations and the uniform prior, with one more control: OUTPUT point (MSE) or mixture with ||(K||) components. The page opens with 1000 events, two layers of 32 neurons, tanh, Adam, ||(\eta||) = 0.003, batches of 64, 100 epochs and a mixture of ||(K||) = 1. MAP A shows the network's mixture for the picks of the test event (68 % and 95 % regions, each component with its weight). MAP B compares it with the truth: the exact posterior is the green shading, the network's 68 % (solid) and 95 % (dashed) regions are the orange lines on top. Each setting trains once and is kept.

data.text/html:
Setup. OUTPUT point, then mixture with ||(K||) = 4. Look for. point: one dot on the line of stations, between the two lobes of the posterior. mixture: a bump in each lobe; compare the orange regions on MAP B with the green posterior. The error is the same for both (29 km, the dashed floor): it scores only the mean.
Setup. ||(K||) = 1, 2, then 4. Look for. ||(K||) = 1 and 2: one ellipse on the line between the lobes, where the source is not. From ||(K||) = 4 a bump in each lobe.
Setup. Drag the test event (star) towards the line of stations, then away. Look for. 5 km from the line the lobes of the exact posterior are 8 km apart and look like one, 30 km from it 55 km apart. It always weighs them equally: a line of stations cannot tell north from south.
Setup. ||(K||) = 4, train prior ridgecrest, press train; then test prior uniform, maps on compare, drag the star into each corner. Look for. In the corners no training event fell, yet the orange regions stay as small as before and miss the star at all four.
Setup. ||(K||) = 4, train as it is; then mute one station at a time. Look for. Unless it is the middle one, the orange regions miss the star although the green posterior still holds it: the mixture's spread is the data's uncertainty, not the network's.

data.text/markdown:
A density can be combined

A point is an answer. A density can take a new prior: what else we know about the source (a mapped fault, a felt report, a second array) as a density ||(\rho_M(\mathbf{m})||). The network was trained on a flat prior, so its answer ||(q||) is the likelihood of the picks, up to a constant. Bayes' rule puts the two together ||[ p(\mathbf{m} \mid \tilde{\mathbf{d}}) \;\propto\; q(\mathbf{m} \mid \tilde{\mathbf{d}})\; \rho_M(\mathbf{m}) ||]The new information is added after training, as in variational prior replacement (Zhao and Curtis, 2024): no new network, no retraining, one multiplication and a normalisation on a grid. A point cannot do this. The mean between two lobes stays between them, however clearly a fault says which lobe is right.

Why a network, when the grid is exact?

The exact posterior of the playground is cheap for two unknowns: it is what we checked the network against. The price comes with more unknowns. A grid with ||(n||) nodes per axis has ||(n^d||) nodes for ||(d||) unknowns, while a mixture of ||(K||) components has ||(K\,(1 + d + d(d+1)/2)||) numbers, ||(6K||) for ||(d = 2||). And the network never needs the likelihood, only a simulator: wherever we can simulate pairs ||((\mathbf{m}, \tilde{\mathbf{d}})||) we can train one. This is neural posterior estimation.

Further reading

Simulate pairs, train a network to output a density, apply it to data: neural posterior estimation (simulation-based inference). Mixture density networks in geophysics: Meier, Curtis and Trampert (2007), crustal thickness; Käufl et al. (2014), earthquake sources. Background: Papamakarios and Murray (2016); Cranmer, Brehmer and Louppe (2020). Changing what a trained posterior assumes, without retraining: Zhao and Curtis (2024).
